title: Physical & Data Link Layer
summary: Bits on wires and frames between neighbors — how data gets from one cable port to the next.

blocks.markdown:
The bottom two layers of the [osi-tcpip-models](osi-tcpip-models) stack handle the raw journey from one cable port to the next.

- **Physical layer** — puts bits on a medium as electrical, optical, or radio signals.
- **Data link layer** — wraps those bits into **frames** and delivers them node-to-node.
- Each layer solves one job; together they let higher layers ignore hardware details.

blocks.subTitle: Two layers, two jobs
blocks.markdown:
Quick reference.

| Layer | OSI # | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Physical | 1 | Signals on medium |
| Data Link | 2 | Node-to-node frames |

Layer 3 (Network) and above rely on these two to handle the hardware.

The **physical layer** is the hardware level: cables, antennas, voltages, light pulses.

- It defines connectors, pin layouts, signal levels, and bit timing.
- It does **not** interpret bits — it only moves them.
- A broken cable is a physical-layer problem; a wrong MAC address is not.

This layer is why you can plug an Ethernet cable in any direction and it works.

blocks.subTitle: Transmission media
blocks.markdown:
Three families of transmission media.

- **Copper wire** (twisted-pair, coaxial) — electrical signals. Cheap, standard Ethernet (Cat5/6). Degrades over distance.
- **Fiber optic** — light pulses through glass. Long distances, very high bandwidth, immune to interference.
- **Wireless** (Wi-Fi, cellular) — radio waves. Shared medium; obstacles and interference reduce speed.

Media choice sets the speed ceiling for that link.

blocks.subTitle: Bits as signals
blocks.markdown:
A **bit** (0 or 1) must become a physical signal to travel a medium.

- Copper: voltage high = 1, low = 0 (simplified).
- Fiber: light pulse present = 1, absent = 0.
- Wireless: a radio frequency shift encodes the bit.

**Bandwidth** (bits per second) is how many bits the medium can carry per second. **Latency** is the delay for the first bit to arrive — bandwidth and latency are separate concerns.

The **data link layer** takes a raw bit stream and turns it into something meaningful between **directly connected nodes** (one hop).

It does four things:
- **Framing** — wraps bits into structured packets called frames.
- **Addressing** — uses MAC addresses to name the sender and receiver.
- **Error detection** — checks for bit-flip errors (CRC).
- **Access control** — decides who transmits on a shared medium.

It is node-to-node, not end-to-end. IP handles end-to-end.

blocks.subTitle: MAC addresses
blocks.markdown:
A **MAC (Media Access Control) address** is a 48-bit hardware address burned into every network interface card.

- Written as six hex pairs: `AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF`.
- Assigned by the manufacturer; first three bytes = vendor OUI.
- Used only within one local network segment — routers do not forward MAC addresses.

Every NIC has a MAC; a laptop with Wi-Fi and Ethernet has two.

blocks.subTitle: MAC vs IP address
blocks.markdown:
Two different addresses, two different scopes.

| Property | MAC address | IP address |
|---|---|---|
| Layer | Data link (L2) | Network (L3) |
| Scope | Local segment only | End-to-end globally |

- MAC is **hardware, permanent** (usually). IP is **logical, assigned** by a network admin or DHCP.
- A frame carries both: MAC gets it across one hop, IP tells it the final destination.

See [ipv4-addressing](ipv4-addressing) for IP details.

blocks.subTitle: Framing
blocks.markdown:
A **frame** is the data link layer's packet. It wraps the network layer's IP packet with extra fields the link needs.

A typical Ethernet frame contains:
- **Destination MAC** and **Source MAC** — who to deliver to and who sent it.
- **EtherType** — signals what's inside (e.g. IPv4, ARP).
- **Payload** — the IP packet.
- **CRC** — a checksum; receiver rejects a frame with a bad CRC.

Frames are discarded at each hop; new ones are built for the next.

blocks.subTitle: Ethernet
blocks.markdown:
**Ethernet** is the dominant wired LAN standard (IEEE 802.3). It defines both physical-layer signaling and the data-link frame format.

- Speeds: 10 Mbps → 10 Gbps+ depending on cable generation.
- Uses MAC addresses for local delivery.
- Originally a shared bus (all devices heard all traffic); modern Ethernet uses **switches** to isolate traffic.

Wi-Fi (802.11) is Ethernet's wireless equivalent; it uses the same MAC address concept.

A **switch** is a [network-devices](network-devices) that forwards frames only to the correct port using a **MAC address table**.

<<< Image: A switch in the center with 4 hosts (A, B, C, D) connected by lines to individual ports. A table beside the switch shows two columns: MAC Address and Port. Each host's MAC maps to its port number. An arrow labeled 'frame for B' goes from host A → switch → port for B only, not to C or D. Clean diagram, blue/grey, generous whitespace. >>>

**How the switch learns:**
1. A frame arrives on port 3 from MAC `AA:BB`.
2. Switch records: `AA:BB → port 3` in its table.
3. Next frame destined for `AA:BB` goes only to port 3.
4. Unknown destination → flood all ports (except the source).

**ARP (Address Resolution Protocol)** maps an IP address to a MAC address within a local network.

**Why needed:** to send a frame, you need the destination's MAC. You know the IP (from DNS or config), but not the MAC.

<<< Image: Three hosts (A, B, C) on a LAN. Host A sends a broadcast labeled 'ARP Request: who has 192.168.1.5? Tell AA:BB'. Arrows go from A to B and A to C. Only host B (which owns 192.168.1.5) replies with a unicast arrow back to A labeled 'ARP Reply: 192.168.1.5 is at CC:DD'. Host A stores this in its ARP cache. Simple, clean, blue arrows. >>>

- ARP request is a **broadcast** — all devices on the segment receive it.
- Only the owner of that IP replies with its MAC.
- The result is cached in the **ARP cache** to avoid repeating the broadcast.

Two important scopes on a network:

- **Collision domain** — the set of devices that can cause a collision if they transmit at the same time. Each switch port is its own collision domain (switches eliminate collisions between ports).
- **Broadcast domain** — the set of devices that receive a broadcast frame. A switch does NOT break broadcast domains — all ports in the same VLAN share one.

A **router** breaks both: it separates collision domains AND broadcast domains.

blocks.subTitle: CSMA/CD
blocks.markdown:
**CSMA/CD (Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Collision Detection)** was the original Ethernet access method for shared bus networks.

- **Carrier Sense** — listen before transmitting; if the medium is busy, wait.
- **Multiple Access** — multiple devices share the same medium.
- **Collision Detection** — if two transmit at once and signals collide, both stop, wait a random backoff time, then retry.

Modern full-duplex switches give each device a dedicated link, so CSMA/CD is largely obsolete — but the concept still appears in exams.

Common mix-ups:

- **"Switches break broadcast domains."** No — switches forward broadcasts. Only routers (and VLANs) stop them.
- **"MAC is permanent."** It can be software-spoofed. "Hardware-burned" means it's the factory default, not immutable.
- **"ARP is only at startup."** ARP runs whenever the cache expires or a new IP is contacted — ongoing.
- **"Physical and data link are the same."** No: physical moves bits; data link gives them structure and addresses.

blocks.subTitle: MAC vs IP address
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is a MAC address and how does it differ from an IP address?**

A **MAC address** is a 48-bit hardware identifier on a NIC, used for delivery within a local network segment. An **IP address** is a logical address used for end-to-end routing across networks.

MAC is layer 2 (link-local); IP is layer 3 (global). A frame carries both: MAC routes the hop, IP routes the full journey.

blocks.subTitle: What does ARP do
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What does ARP do and when is it triggered?**

**ARP** resolves an IP address to a MAC address on a local network. It is triggered whenever a host needs to send a frame to an IP it doesn't have a MAC for (cache miss). It broadcasts "who has IP X?" and the owner replies with its MAC. The result is cached to avoid repeat broadcasts.

blocks.subTitle: Switch vs hub
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: How does a switch differ from a hub?**

A **hub** is a dumb repeater: it broadcasts every frame out all ports. All devices share one collision domain and see all traffic.

A **switch** learns MAC addresses and forwards frames only to the correct port. Each port is its own collision domain — devices don't compete, and bandwidth is not wasted.

blocks.subTitle: Collision vs broadcast domain
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is the difference between a collision domain and a broadcast domain?**

A **collision domain** is where simultaneous transmissions collide. Switches break it per port — each port is isolated. A **broadcast domain** is where a broadcast frame reaches every device. Switches do not break this; a router (or VLAN) is needed to limit broadcast scope.

blocks.subTitle: Why frames are rebuilt per hop
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why is a new frame built at every router hop?**

Frames are local — a MAC address only means something on its own network segment. When a router forwards a packet, it strips the old frame (which carried the packet to this router) and builds a new frame using the MAC of the next hop. The IP packet inside is unchanged; only the frame wrapper changes each hop.
